draft.title: High Court cases on law-making powers
card: The High Court of Australia decides what the Constitution means. When it rules on a Commonwealth law, it can decide that parliament had the power to make it, or that it did not.
Section 90 says only the Commonwealth may impose duties of excise, which are taxes on the production or sale of goods. States cannot impose them.
In Ha v New South Wales (1997), the High Court read excise widely. It held that state licence fees on tobacco, based on the value of tobacco sold, were excises. The state fees were therefore invalid.

The ruling cut the states' power to raise their own revenue and left more power with the Commonwealth. A court decision can shift power between the states and the Commonwealth without any change to the wording of the Constitution.
draft.remember: The High Court's reading of the Constitution can shift power between the Commonwealth and the states.

a.q: What did the High Court's decision in Ha v New South Wales do to the balance of power?
opts: It limited state taxing power and favoured the Commonwealth
It gave the states more power to tax goods
It changed the wording of section 90
It made state and Commonwealth taxing powers equal
a.why: The Court read excise widely, so the state tobacco licence fees were invalid. That limited the states' ability to raise revenue and left the power with the Commonwealth. The Court did not change the wording of section 90, as it only interpreted it.
a.clue: Ask who is allowed to impose excise under section 90.

b.q: A High Court ruling reads the meaning of excise more widely than before. A state had charged a fee on each litre of fuel sold. What is the most likely effect?
opts: The fee may be invalid, which limits the state's revenue
The fee is valid, because the state gets more power
The Constitution is amended, so the fee becomes lawful
The Commonwealth loses power to tax fuel as well
b.why: A wider meaning of excise means more state taxes can be caught by section 90, which reserves excise for the Commonwealth. A fee charged on goods sold may therefore be invalid. The Court interprets the Constitution and does not amend it, since changing the wording needs a referendum.
b.clue: Only the Commonwealth may impose excise, so a wider meaning catches more state taxes.

a.best: It limited state taxing power and favoured the Commonwealth

b.best: The fee may be invalid, which limits the state's revenue

problems.detail: The right option stands out. It is the longest and the only one with a qualifier ('may'), so a student could pick it without knowing the idea.
The clue gives the answer away. It says a wider meaning 'catches more state taxes', which leaves only the 'fee may be invalid' option as plausible.

a.q: What did the High Court's decision in Ha v New South Wales do to the balance of power?
opts: It limited state taxing power, favouring the Commonwealth
It gave the states more power to tax goods such as tobacco
It changed the wording of section 90 of the Constitution
It made state and Commonwealth taxing powers equal
a.why: The Court read excise widely, so the state tobacco licence fees were invalid. That limited the states' ability to raise revenue and left the power with the Commonwealth. The Court did not change the wording of section 90, as it only interpreted it.
a.clue: Ask who is allowed to impose excise under section 90.

b.q: The High Court reads section 90 widely, as it did in Ha v New South Wales. A state charges a fee on each litre of fuel sold. What follows?
opts: The fee is invalid, because it counts as an excise
The fee is valid, because states can set their own taxes
The Court amends section 90, so the fee stays valid
The Commonwealth loses its own power to tax fuel
b.why: Under a wide reading, a fee on each litre of fuel sold is a tax on the sale of goods, so it is an excise. Section 90 gives excise to the Commonwealth only, so the state fee is invalid. States can raise some taxes of their own, but not excise, and the Court interprets section 90 rather than changing it.
b.clue: Is a fee on each litre sold a tax on the sale of goods?
